All 100 simulations are used. The best design scores a mean L/D of **116.6**, which is 25% above NACA 4412 (93.5).

## Best design
**u = [0.38, 0.54, 0.58, 0.74, 0.41, 0.67, 0.64]**

This works out to thickness weights a0 ≈ 0.72, a2 ≈ 1.04 and a3 ≈ 1.11, and camber weights b ≈ [0.196, 0.064, 0.168, 0.156]. Maximum thickness is at about 40% chord. Maximum camber is about 3.3% at 56% chord.

| CL | alpha | cd | L/D | cm |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.4 | −0.47° | 0.00520 | 76.9 | −0.111 |
| 0.6 | 1.55° | 0.00489 | 122.7 | −0.105 |
| 0.8 | 2.88° | 0.00532 | 150.3 | −0.118 |

## What I learned about the design space
- **Drag is almost flat across the three lift targets (about 0.0049 to 0.0053).** Since L/D is CL divided by drag, the CL = 0.4 point is stuck near 77 and the mean is set mostly by the 0.6 and 0.8 points. Good designs keep laminar flow over a wide range of lift without letting drag rise at CL = 0.8.
- **Camber level involves a clear trade-off, and the best is about 3.3–3.5%.** At 2.5% camber, drag at CL = 0.8 rises. At 4.5% or more, the airfoil runs at negative alpha at CL = 0.4 and drag on the lower surface rises (cd 0.0065–0.007). Either way the mean drops. The useful window is narrow.
- **How the camber is spread matters about as much as how much there is.** The best shape had a fairly high leading-edge weight (b0), a dip in the second weight (b1), and most of the camber in the rear half (b2, b3). This gave about 3 more L/D than a uniform camber line. Pushing it to extremes made it worse: with b0 at its maximum and b1 low, drag at CL = 0.8 went back up to about 0.0057.
- **Leading-edge bluntness (a0) is the most sensitive setting.** A sharp edge (u0 = 0.1) separated at CL = 0.8 (cd 0.020). A blunt edge (u0 = 0.7) moved maximum thickness forward to 24% and cost about 20 L/D. The sweet spot was u0 ≈ 0.35–0.40, which puts maximum thickness near 40% chord and keeps a favourable pressure gradient over a long laminar run.
- **Aft thickness (a2) and trailing-edge wedge (a3) both pay off in moderation.** More aft thickness helped up to u1 ≈ 0.55–0.6 and then raised drag. A larger wedge cut drag at CL = 0.4 but raised it at 0.8 by moving loading toward the trailing edge. Combining thin aft thickness with a large wedge (u1 = 0.4, u2 = 0.8) failed to converge at CL = 0.4, the only failure in the whole run.
- **The optimum is a broad, flat plateau.** The last 30 or so designs all scored between 115.5 and 116.6. Differences there are close to XFoil's own run-to-run variation, so the gain from further fine-tuning is probably under 1 L/D. The price of the aft camber is a nose-down pitching moment of about −0.11, compared with roughly −0.1 for NACA 4412. This objective doesn't penalise that.
